title: Is more devolved democracy the answer to delivery of the International Education Strategy?
summary:
This blog was kindly authored by James Pitman, Adviser to the Education Strategy Action Group and Managing Director (UK and Europe) for Study Group.  The International Education Strategy has a laudable target of £40 billion in education exports by 2030, yet the trajectory of international student recruitment remains under significant pressure. The post Is more devolved democracy the answer to delivery of the International Education Strategy?  appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by James Pitman, Adviser to the Education Strategy Action Group and Managing Director (UK and Europe) for Study Group.

The International Education Strategy has a laudable target of £40 billion in education exports by 2030, yet the trajectory of international student recruitment remains under significant pressure. The removal of dependent visas, tightening of Basic Compliance Assessment (BCA) metrics, visa brakes on a number of countries and an alarming rise in visa rejections are all biting.

The problem is that the Government’s increasing reliance on transnational education (TNE), which currently represents a relatively small proportion of the value of higher education exports, is not going to redeem that position. TNE is undoubtedly a major opportunity for the UK, but it cannot simply replace the economic value of students coming here to study. One can only conclude that, without a change in direction, the International Education Strategy target will be missed. And this in a global market where many of the UK’s historically major competitors are themselves in retreat.

The net loss of international students since 2023 has already led to a significant reduction in inward investment, economic activity, jobs, income to the Exchequer and, of course, soft power. The estimated reduction in international students studying in the UK between 2022/23 and 2024/25 was 76,000, and there is a real risk of further reductions when the figures for 2025/26 become available.

Drawing on recently published HEPI estimates of the economic contribution of international students, we can estimate that the loss of those 76,000 students represents some £7 billion in net economic activity, £2.5 billion in contributions to the Exchequer and £2 billion in inward investment, while potentially putting 53,000 jobs at risk, probably around half of them in local economies around universities. These are estimates of economic impact rather than confirmed losses, but they give some indication of the scale of what is at stake. This is not exactly the ‘good growth in every postcode’ that the Burnham administration is promising.

The contradiction at the heart of policy

One could argue that the reason for this dichotomy between the level of aspiration in the International Education Strategy and the reality is that the Home Office is not a co-owner of the Strategy.

Indeed, the Home Office has an overriding single-issue strategic imperative: reducing net migration. And because international students continue to be, erroneously in my view, counted in those numbers, they feel the full brunt of efforts to reduce migration.

Of course, the integrity of the student visa system matters, and no one is suggesting compliance should be weakened. But the economic consequences of immigration restrictions do not appear to receive anything like the same weight as their anticipated impact on migration numbers.

The impact assessments accompanying Home Office policy changes rarely seem to capture the full damage that may be caused to universities, local economies and employment. You will not often see a serious assessment of the risk to jobs in university towns and cities, for instance, when restrictions are introduced.

Yet these consequences are very real. And perhaps there is another way forward, because it is the communities in and around higher education institutions across the UK that stand to gain or lose depending on decisions made by civil servants in Marsham Street, London.

This raises a fundamental question of democratic accountability. Why should decisions with such significant consequences for local economies be taken almost entirely in Whitehall, with so little say for the communities most affected?

Could greater devolution offer a way forward?

The Prime Minister is keen to drive growth through devolution and one of the great growth opportunities open to the UK could be unlocked by greater devolution of powers over international students to devolved administrations and, perhaps, to regional authorities across England.

From recent conversations with the respective responsible ministers, it is clear that Scotland and Wales already recognise the importance of international education to their economies and have sought greater flexibility in how they attract and retain international students. The proposed International Student Levy, only applying to England, is a further illustration of the different policy choices being made across the UK. After all, imposing what amounts to an export tax is hardly the most obvious way to encourage growth in one of our most successful export sectors.

The devolved Governments in Scotland and Wales understand that international education is not simply about university finances. It is about jobs, investment, skills, population and the economic prospects of their communities.

And there is no reason why the same arguments should not apply to the English regions.

One of the advantages of greater devolved responsibility would be to make local communities, and their elected representatives, more directly responsible for the situation international students find themselves in.

This should lead to more joined-up planning between local government, universities, accommodation providers, transport, the NHS, employers and others.

It was for this reason that I proposed the introduction of regional international student number targets in the International Education Strategy, during consultations with the sector carried out by civil servants. But, of course, we did not even get a national target.

Regional ambitions for international student growth could be linked to wider economic strategies, with local leaders accountable for both the opportunities and the practical implications.

There is also a legitimate question about the Immigration Health Surcharge that international students pay every year. Are the additional resources available to health services in the areas where international students actually live and study proportionate to the contributions they make? I imagine both devolved governments, and indeed many English regional leaders, would be interested in the answer.

The point is that international education should not be something that happens to local communities as a consequence of decisions taken elsewhere. It should be something they have a meaningful role in shaping.

Why not devolve the post-study offering too?

Clearly, the types of skills in shortage differ from country to country and region to region, so it makes absolute sense to allow greater devolved responsibility for addressing these needs through international education. This is particularly relevant to the post-study offering.

There is precedent for this in Scotland with the Fresh Talent: Working in Scotland Scheme of 2005, and more recently the Scottish Government’s lobbying for a Scottish Graduate Visa.

Australia has also experimented with differentiated post-study work opportunities, including longer periods for graduates in particular fields. Why should we not consider something similar here?

A devolved government or regional authority might, for instance, be able to offer enhanced post-study work opportunities to international graduates in areas facing particular skills shortages, perhaps through a longer period of permission to work where graduates take up employment in the region, just as is currently available for PhD students.

Imagine the potential value to regions struggling to retain highly skilled graduates, or seeking to develop new industries in engineering, technology, healthcare and other priority areas.

Of course, immigration remains a reserved matter, and there would need to be a UK-wide framework with appropriate safeguards. A student visa is linked to a sponsoring institution and its approved places of study, but this is not the same as restricting all subsequent movement or employment to a particular region. Any geographically linked graduate visa would therefore need careful design. But these are practical questions to be addressed, not reasons to dismiss the idea.

We could begin with pilots in Scotland, Wales and interested English regions, assessing their impact on graduate retention, skills shortages, economic growth and compliance before considering wider implementation, including areas not yet part of mayoral regions.

There is no reason why greater regional flexibility should be incompatible with a coherent national immigration system. Indeed, one might argue that a system which better reflects the economic and demographic needs of different parts of the UK would be a considerable improvement on the one-size-fits-all approach we have today.

Democracy, accountability and public confidence

There is another important advantage to greater devolution, and it goes beyond economics. Decisions by devolved governments and regional authorities relating to the flow of international students into their communities, and the offering both during and after study, would necessarily need to be justified through local democratic processes.

This would create opportunities for much more positive and informed discussions about international students, explaining the specific benefits of recruitment and retention to local communities while also addressing legitimate concerns about housing, infrastructure and public services.

It would make local political leaders accountable not simply for attracting more international students, but for ensuring that their communities benefit and are seen to benefit, from their presence.

This contrasts sharply with the experience of immigration policy tightening over the last 15 years. Successive governments have frequently justified restrictions through selective and sometimes anecdotal examples of perceived abuse of the student visa system by relatively small numbers of international students.

The cumulative effect of this toxic drip has been the steady erosion of public support for one of the UK’s most successful export sectors, with these concerns then amplified by certain politicians for their own short-term gain.

Yet ask the businesses in university towns and cities what the loss of international students means to them. Ask employers about the value of graduates with international experience and specialist skills. Ask researchers about the importance of attracting talent from around the world. There is a very different story to be told.

Greater local democratic involvement could help ensure that this story is heard, alongside a proper discussion about the responsibilities that come with international recruitment.

It might also help to move international education away from the increasingly unhelpful national debate in which students are viewed primarily as contributors to immigration statistics, rather than as people making a substantial contribution to our economy, universities and communities.

A challenge for No. 10 (North and South)

We all know that the opportunity for growth exists. The UK’s universities remain internationally respected, demand for high-quality education continues to grow around the world, and the economic and diplomatic benefits of international education are considerable. As the Prime Minister himself said of his work in Manchester:

We could not have done what we did here in the last 10 or more years without having the universities right with us, and I mean right with us, developing the thinking, the ambition for what we could be, and I know that applies elsewhere as well.

But unless this Government decouples international students from the immigration debate, which I see little evidence of, we will continue to face the same contradiction between our export ambitions and the policies that undermine them. Perhaps gradual devolution of powers over international students as an economic driver offers another way forward.

This need not begin with wholesale devolution of immigration policy. Regional international education strategies, a greater say for devolved governments and regional authorities in national policy, and carefully designed pilots for geographically linked graduate visas would be a sensible start.

The important point is to recognise that the economic benefits and consequences of international student recruitment are not distributed evenly across the UK, and that the communities most affected should have a greater say in the decisions being made.

If devolution is about allowing places to shape their own economic futures, international education surely deserves to be part of that conversation. So, if the Prime Minister genuinely wants growth in every postcode achieved hand-in-hand with universities, perhaps he should start by asking the people responsible for those postcodes and the institutions of higher education that underpin their success, what international education could do for them.

title: Global Higher Education Enrollments ‘to Peak by 2036’
summary:
Global Higher Education Enrollments ‘to Peak by 2036’ Susan H. Greenberg Wed, 11/25/2026 - 03:00 AM Africa’s growing youth population is unlikely to offset the demographic dip that will empty classrooms, says new report. Byline(s) Jack Grove for Times Higher Education Global Higher Education Enrollments ‘to Peak by 2036’
Susan H. Greenberg Wed, 11/25/2026 - 03:00 AM

Africa’s growing youth population is unlikely to offset the demographic dip that will empty classrooms, says new report.

Byline(s)
Jack Grove for Times Higher Education
full_text:
“Peak global higher education” is only a decade away, as youth populations will drop sharply in most countries starting in 2036, says a new report.

Using medium-term population projections from the United Nations on the world’s 50 most populous nations, the study by Toronto-based consultancy Higher Education Strategy Associates explains the overall 18-to-21 population will continue rising until 2035, with just a handful of countries (including France, the U.S. and India) having their youth populations shrink.

But, from this point, many countries will start to see sharp declines. The fall will be particularly precipitous in China, where the youth population is expected to fall from 69.5 million to 33.5 million in the decade leading up to 2046, a 52 percent decline.

Russia, Japan, Turkey, Iran and Spain will also witness reductions of at least 20 percent in their 18-to-21 population over this period, says the report, published Nov. 24.

The U.K., France, Italy and Brazil will see youth population decreases of between 10 percent and 19 percent over this time frame, with Canada, India and the U.S. likely to see a fall between 1 percent and 9 percent.

Over all, 31 of the world’s 50 most populous countries—including all of those located in Europe and the Americas—will have youth populations in decline over this period, says the study, which also examines whether higher economic growth in “poor but increasingly populous countries” in Africa and Asia might generate enough enrollment growth to offset declining youth populations elsewhere.

Angola’s youth population is set to grow 84 percent by the mid-2030s, for instance, and Tanzania’s increase is “not far behind at 73 percent,” while seven sub-Saharan African countries are projected to see enrollments grow by 50 percent or more.

While these economies are likely to grow significantly, this growth and resulting increase in international student mobility will be “nowhere near enough to offset the very significant drops in enrollment in richer countries, particularly China,” the report says.

“The era of global expansion of higher education, which has been a defining feature of the sector since the end of World War II, seems likely to be coming to an end,” predicts the report, written by Alex Usher, the consultancy’s president, concluding: “Peak higher education is in sight.”

Speaking to Times Higher Education, Usher said the countries on the receiving end of demographic decline needed to have “honest discussions about how to shrink the system” and consider “what stays, what goes, and which institutions [should remain].”

“Many countries—South Korea, Poland and Greece—seem to be under the impression they can keep their systems from deflating by increasing international student numbers. Possibly a few of them will succeed but they can’t all do so,” he said.

“It will be important to have discussions about how to keep systems and institutions viable as they shrink,” he continued, noting, “Places like Taiwan are dealing with this now and coming up with plans to shrink strategically. At the national level, that might be a good thing, but there will be a lot of tensions at specific institutions, particularly the less selective ones.”

There will be repercussions for science because “total research output has for the last 80 years largely been a function of the number of people employed in universities,” added Usher. “Total researcher numbers will plateau not long after total student numbers,” he said.

The report’s findings should force developed nations to consider how they are going to manage these declines in youth populations, with several European countries having begun to experience such dips. Ukraine’s higher education sector is “barely half the size it was 15 years ago” and there have been “major declines in Poland and Romania” in recent years. Turkey’s student numbers have fallen by nearly 25 percent in the past five years, the report notes.

“It is simply going to get harder for institutions in developed countries to grow their way out of trouble through importing international students, or some form of transnational education. Not impossible, by any means, but individual institutions will be fighting over a shrinking pie come 2035 or so.”

title: Syracuse University adds AI review to undergraduate admissions
summary: The technology will conduct the first review of applicants’ transcripts, while the final stages will “remain entirely human,” a senior official said.
full_text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Dive Brief:

Syracuse University will use generative artificial intelligence in its undergraduate admissions process beginning this application cycle, it announced Friday.

AI will “conduct the first review”of applicants’ transcripts, and admissions readers will be able to ask the AI questions about prospective students’ packets, according to the selective New York institution.Humans will conduct the entirety of the final stages of the process, and AI won’t make admission decisions, the university said.

Syracuse tested its AI process using previous application data scrubbed of personal information. The universitydid not immediately respond to questions Tuesday, including about what AI software it will be using.

Dive Insight:

Syracuse is one of the latest and most prominent examples of colleges turning to AI in the admissions process. The private university will use AI for “synthesizing grades into a uniform scale, gathering information on the student’s high school and drafting a short summary to attach to the application.” The admissions team will continue review all applications.

“To be clear, AI does not admit or deny any student,” Denny Nicholson, Syracuse’s dean of admissions, said in a statement. “Every decision is made by a member of the admissions team, and later stages of review, including admitting the class, remain entirely human.”

Applicant data is stored securely and is not used to train AI models, the university said.

Syracuse expects AI to free up admissions counselors to work directly with applicants and to speed up the decision-making timeline.

“These tools augment the work of our admissions team; they do not automate it,” Jeff Rubin, senior vice president and chief digital officer at Syracuse, said in a statement. “We have tested them carefully, and we will continue to evaluate them to ensure they serve our team and the students we serve.”

Syracuse is facing a projected budget deficit and is reviewing its executive and administrative roles to rightsize its workforce.

While Syracuse did not cite reduced cost as a motivating factor for AI use, higher education and other sectors have turned to automation to trim budgets and conserve resources.

Some colleges that use AI in admissions have also addressed how applicants can use the technology.

In September, the Georgia Institute of Technologyannounced that it would incorporate AI into its admissions process at several “pain points,” as described by one senior official.

The technology now assists admissions officials in reviewing transcripts and credit transfers, cutting the latter process to “a fraction of the time.”

On its website, Georgia Tech calls AI a potentially “powerful and valuable” tool for applicants and released guidance for its acceptable use.

Prospective students can use AI “to brainstorm, edit, and refine” ideas but “should not copy and paste content” they didn’t create themselves into their applications, Georgia Tech said in a statement.

The institution also said AI can be a “helpful collaborator” for students who don’t have any other sources of assistance in the application process.

The University of Pennsylvania provides guidance on AI for its notoriously selective admissions process.

Applicants can use tools, including AI, to organize their thoughts and check grammar without violating the university’s policies. But “submitting work, ideas, or experiences that aren't authentically” theirs is disqualifying, the Ivy League institution said.

“Here’s a simple test: if you couldn't explain, in an interview or conversation, how you arrived at what you wrote, or speak to it in your own words, it isn't ready to submit,” the university’s guidance said.

On the same webpage, Penn said it uses AI in admissions for “administrative rather than evaluative” processes. They include confirming an application is complete and accurate, “ensuring consistency of the understanding and interpretation of transcript and grading scales,” reviewing transfer credits and assisting with documentation processing. Penn staff members review those results before they affect students’ files, it said.

Like Syracuse, Georgia Tech and Penn said admissions decisions remain in the hands of humans.

But not all colleges are incorporating AI into admissions.

At a conference last month, admissions officials from the University of Michigan, Rice University, and the University of Georgia said their institutions do not use AI to review applications.

Rice’s executive director of admission, Charles Murphy, also expressed concern about trying to use AI to detect AI in students’ applications.

His team enters Rice’s essay prompts into generative AI to get a baseline of what an AI response could look like, he said. But he’s wary of the detection software’s likelihood to flag false positives.

title: Highest MP turnover rate in decades making for byelection bonanza this Parliament
summary: A slew of MP resignations is putting this Parliament on track to have the most byelections this soon after a general election in over half a century.
full_text:
A slew of MP resignations is putting this Parliament on track to have the most byelections this soon after a general election in over half a century.

It will be 560 days since the 2025 election when voters in six ridings go to the polls on Dec. 7. That will bring the total number of byelections held since the last general election to 13 — and that doesn't include the riding of Parry Sound-Muskoka where current MP Scott Aitchison has signalled his intention to resign in the coming weeks.

The last time there were more byelections in that short amount of time was after the 1949 election. That year, newly minted Liberal Leader Louis St. Laurent won his first election as prime minister and by October of 1950 he had called 16 byelections.

Jonathan Malloy, a political science professor at Carleton University, says there are some similarities between the current Parliament and the one elected in 1949, given St. Laurent and Prime Minister Mark Carney both returned the Liberal Party to power after taking over leadership.

But beyond that, he told CBC News that "the political conditions were rather different back then."

"This is a very unusual Parliament and, to me, it's because of the unexpected election results in April 2025," Malloy said, noting that Carney's Liberals were behind in the polls when he took over the party.

"In both cases you do have a prime minister succeeding another one and successfully winning elections. That's the obvious connection. But on the other hand, the 1949 election was not radically different from what people had been expecting, say a year or two before."

Ironically, there is a near identical situation between the Terrebonne byelection held earlier this year and the 1950 byelection in what was then the Nova Scotia riding of Annapolis-Kings: both results from the preceding general election were declared void due to issues around vote counting.

But besides that case, the reasons for the rapid turnover rate in the 21st Parliament appear to be quite different from the current crop of MPs who have recently left their seats.

Of the 16 MPs who vacated in the first few years following the 1949 vote, most were appointed to judicial or Senate positions. A handful of seats were also left vacant after five MPs died while in office between October 1949 and October 1950.

Éric Grenier — a polls analyst who noted the byelection trend for his publication, The Writ — told CBC News that the amount of MPs stepping down so far in this Parliament could be "just a bit of a coincidence" because there have been a variety of reasons for their resignations.

Conservative Damien Kurek was the first MP to exit to allow for leader Pierre Poilievre to reclaim a seat. Carney also appointed former MPs Bill Blair and Jonathan Wilkinson to diplomatic posts — and appointed Richard Martel to the Senate.

Four MPs swapped their federal roles for provincial or municipal ones. Larry Brock left to return to his local Crown attorney's office. Former cabinet ministers Steven Guilbeault and Chrystia Freeland left after serving a number of years in the former Trudeau government and Conservative Cathay Wagantall had been on the Opposition benches since 2015.

Malloy said the surprising reversal of Liberal fortunes during the 2025 campaign could have pushed some of those MPs to reassess their career trajectories. He suggested that for Liberals, they may have expected to lose their seats (or move to the Opposition benches) under Trudeau and are "not really comfortable in this new situation" of serving in Carney's government — as was the apparent case with Guilbeault.

For Conservatives, Malloy said there are likely some dashed expectations of forming government.

"Elections have a habit of helping MPs make their career decisions one way or the other," he said.

Grenier said the Liberals attaining a majority in the House earlier this year may have also factored into recent decisions.

"[That] kind of sets everybody's minds to the next four years rather than the next 18 months," he said.

The current slate of byelections may not reach the same levels as seen in the early days of Parliament when MPs were expected to resign and rerun in their riding when they were appointed ministers — a practice that was ended in 1931.

Still, Grenier says it's been a significant amount of byelections so far this parliamentary session.

"It is just kind of remarkable how many there's been," he said.

title: Brazil’s bilingual school boom fuels study abroad ambitions
summary:
The growth of bilingual education in Brazil is creating a new generation of prospective international students, with families increasingly looking beyond the US and scrutinising the return on investment of studying overseas.

The post Brazil’s bilingual school boom fuels study abroad ambitions appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Speaking at The PIE High Brazil in São Paulo, Paulo Moraes, CEO of Inspired Education Brazil, estimated that the country now has more than 3,000 schools offering some form of bilingual education.

Across Inspired’s Brazilian schools with graduating cohorts, around 50% of students include an overseas university among their top three choices, while approximately 20% ultimately study abroad.

Destination preferences are also shifting. Moraes noted that the US accounted for around 40% of overseas destination preferences among its students three years ago, compared with approximately 30% today, with Europe and Canada gaining ground.

However, Isabel Zillig, general manager LATAM at Shorelight, reported a positive experience in the Brazilian market despite negative headlines surrounding US visas, noting that families are increasingly asking sophisticated questions about salaries, career prospects and return on investment.

While the US remains a popular choice, Thassiana Balbino, business development manager for TOEFL iBT in Brazil at ETS, said Canada had recently emerged as its fastest-growing destination market. She attributed students’ growing readiness for overseas higher education to improvements in English-language teaching in Brazilian schools, while pointing to ETS’s partnership with Passage as a way to help more students afford to study abroad.

Mauricio Segura, founder and CEO of GlobalCamps, highlighted a persistent information gap, with many Brazilian families associating international education with expensive, elite US institutions and remaining unaware of more affordable alternatives.

He also identified the next 24 months as a significant recruitment opportunity for Latin America as universities seek to diversify their international student populations.

Meanwhile, Moraes warned that recruiting and retaining qualified teachers capable of delivering subjects in English could determine the pace of Brazil’s internationalisation.

As bilingual education becomes more commonplace, he suggested, the competitive advantage for schools will increasingly lie in their ability to deliver on their international ambitions.

title: End With the Heart: Sustaining Compassionate Connections
summary:
As the semester begins to come to a close, something shifts in the room. The energy changes. There is a quiet mixture of fatigue, anticipation, pressure, and, at times, disconnection. Students are holding many things at once. Deadlines, uncertainty, personal responsibilities, and hopes for what comes next. As faculty, we are often holding just as […]

The post End With the Heart: Sustaining Compassionate Connections  appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
As the semester begins to come to a close, something shifts in the room. The energy changes. There is a quiet mixture of fatigue, anticipation, pressure, and, at times, disconnection. Students are holding many things at once. Deadlines, uncertainty, personal responsibilities, and hopes for what comes next. As faculty, we are often holding just as much.

If we begin our courses with the heart, then we are called to end them the same way.

The final weeks of a course are not simply about finishing content or assigning final grades. They are about how we accompany our students through a meaningful transition. They are about how we hold the learning, the relationships, and the lived experiences that have unfolded over time. Ending with the heart invites us to remain present, to stay relational, and to approach closure with the same compassion that grounded the beginning. This relational approach to teaching echoes hooks’ (1994) vision of education as a practice rooted in connection, presence, and shared humanity.

Returning to Compassion in the Closing Weeks

Compassion, as Gilbert (2009) reminds us, involves an attunement to suffering with a commitment to respond to it. Neff (2003, 2023) expands this understanding by emphasizing self-compassion as the practice of relating to ourselves with kindness, recognizing our shared humanity, and remaining mindfully present with our experiences. Germer (2009) further describes compassion as a moment-to-moment process of turning toward difficulty with care rather than avoidance, allowing us to meet challenges with warmth and understanding.

In the final weeks of a course, this attunement becomes especially important. Students may not always name what they are carrying, but we can often feel it. Increased anxiety. Self-doubt. Exhaustion. A sense of urgency. A feeling of being overwhelmed and overextended.

Ending with the heart means softening into self-kindness, remembering our shared humanity, and staying present with what is, rather than what we wish had been. It is not about removing the challenge but about holding it with care.

Holding the Home Stretch with Intention

The final weeks benefit from clarity and steadiness. When expectations are clearly communicated and thoughtfully organized, students can exhale, even if just a little. A simple roadmap of what remains, paired with reassurance, can reduce uncertainty and support focus.

At the same time, compassion invites us to ask ourselves: What truly matters now? What are the essential learning experiences we want students to carry with them?

When we align our expectations with what is meaningful rather than excessive, we create space for deeper engagement rather than overwhelm. This is not about lowering standards. It is about teaching with intention and discernment.

Staying Connected as Energy Shifts

It is natural for engagement to change as the semester winds down. Students may feel pulled in many directions. Rather than interpreting this as disengagement, we can approach it with curiosity and care.

Inviting students to reflect on their learning can gently reawaken connection. What has stayed with you? What challenged you? Where have you grown?

One simple practice I often use is inviting students into a brief “glow and grow” reflection—naming something they are proud of and something they are continuing to develop. This creates space for both celebration and self-compassion, allowing students to hold their learning with balance and care.

These moments do not need to be complex. Sometimes a brief reflection, a shared conversation, or a pause to acknowledge the collective experience of the semester can bring the room back together.

Naming what is present matters. When we say, “This is a full time for many of us,” we remind students that they are not alone. That sense of shared humanity can be grounding in ways that are often understated but deeply felt.

Tending to Stress with Compassion

The end of the semester can be one of the most stressful periods for students and faculty alike. Bringing small moments of care into our classrooms can make a meaningful difference.

This might look like a brief pause for a breath. A moment to check in. A gentle reminder that it is okay to feel overwhelmed. These practices do not take away from learning. They support it.

Encouraging self-compassion during this time can help students shift how they relate to their own struggles. Rather than moving into cycles of self-criticism, they can begin to meet themselves with kindness and understanding. Research suggests that self-compassion supports emotional resilience and reduces distress (Neff, 2003).

When we model this ourselves, even in small ways, we offer students permission to do the same.

Creating Meaningful Last-Day Experiences

The final class session holds a particular kind of significance. It is a moment of closure, but also of integration.

Rather than filling this time with only final logistics, we can create space for reflection. Inviting students to share what they are taking with them, what mattered, or what they are proud of can be deeply grounding.

There is something powerful about being witnessed at the end of a journey.

Expressions of gratitude can also be meaningful. When we take a moment to acknowledge our students, not only for what they have done but for who they have been in the space, it reinforces their sense of belonging and worth.

Extending Connection Beyond the Final Class

Ending with the heart does not have to stop when the final class session ends.

One practice I have found deeply meaningful is sending a follow-up email to students after the course concludes. In this message, I gently recap our shared journey. I reflect on moments of growth I witnessed, themes that emerged, and the ways students showed up for one another and for themselves.

This is not an evaluation. It is a continuation of the relational space we built together.

Students often carry these reflections with them. Being reminded of their growth, especially in their own words or through moments they may have overlooked, can support their sense of competence, belonging, and self-trust as they move forward.

In many ways, this final outreach becomes a quiet closing circle. A way of saying, “I saw you. Your presence mattered here.”

Holding Imperfection with Care

Not every course unfolds in the way we imagined. There may be moments we wish we could revisit. Times when connection felt harder to access. Endings that feel incomplete.

Ending with the heart includes making space for this.

We can acknowledge what was challenging while also honoring what was meaningful. We can reflect on our own learning alongside our students. This kind of honesty, held with care, models growth, humility, and compassion.

It reminds students that learning is not about perfection. It is about presence, effort, and continued becoming.

Closing the Relational Space

A course is more than a series of assignments. It is a shared relational experience.

As we close, we have the opportunity to affirm each student’s presence in that experience. Sometimes this happens through feedback. Sometimes through a brief note or class announcement. Sometimes through a simple, genuine acknowledgment in real time.

These moments stay with students.

Ending with the heart means recognizing that how we close matters just as much as how we begin. It is an opportunity to leave students with a felt sense of being seen, valued, and capable of continuing forward.

Ending With the Heart

When we approach the final weeks of a course with compassion, we shift the experience from one of completion to one of integration.

We are not simply finishing. We are honoring.

We are honoring the learning, the effort, the challenges, and the relationships that have unfolded. We are holding space for transition with care and intention.

And in doing so, we remind our students, and ourselves, that education at its best is not only about what we know, but about how we show up for one another along the way.

Dr. Mindith R. Rahmat, PsyD, is a core faculty member at Antioch University, where she specializes in compassion-focused pedagogy, trauma-sensitive mindfulness, and mindful self-compassion. With over 25 years of experience teaching yoga, meditation, and holistic wellness practices, she integrates these methodologies into her classroom, fostering equitable, intentional learning environments that promote well-being, resilience, and flourishing.

References

title: heise-Angebot: Public IT 2027: c't sucht Vorträge aus dem öffentlichen Sektor
summary: Die c't-Konferenz Public IT dreht sich um IT und Digitalisierung im öffentlichen Sektor. Aktuell sucht die Redaktion praxisnahe Vorträge.
full_text:
Die zweite Auflage der c’t-Konferenz Public IT findet am 28. und 29. April im Hannover Congress Centrum (HCC) statt. Für das Programm sucht die Redaktion von c’t praxisnahe Vorträge von Menschen, die im öffentlichen Sektor IT- oder Digitalisierungsprojekte leiten und umsetzen. Wir freuen uns insbesondere über Speaker, die selbst im öffentlichen Sektor beschäftigt sind.

Weiterlesen nach der Anzeige

Inhaltlich fokussiert sich das Programm auf die beiden Schwerpunkte „Automatisierung & KI“ sowie „Cloud & Souveränität“. Beiträge können sich unter anderem mit folgenden Themen befassen:

On-Premise, Cloud oder Multi-Cloud: Souveräne Infrastruktur

Cloud-Transformation: Container, CI/CD und Orchestrierung

Souveräne KI-Infrastruktur

Souveräne Arbeitsplatzlösungen

Datenschutz, Datensicherheit und Recht

Automatisierung und Prozessoptimierung

LowCode & NoCode

Generative KI / Agentische KI

Ende-zu-Ende-Digitalisierung

Registermodernisierung/Register-as-a-Service

Vorschläge können bis zum 13. Dezember 2026 über die Webseite der Public IT eingereicht werden. Die c’t-Redaktion freut sich auch über Vorschläge zu weiteren Themen, die in den Kontext der Public IT passen. Erfahrungsberichte aus Projekten sind besonders gern gesehen. Das Programm wird Mitte Januar veröffentlicht.

Konkrete Umsetzung im Vordergrund

Eine Besonderheit der Public IT bleibt die technische Tiefe: Hier geht es nicht um abstrakte politische Ziele, sondern um die konkrete Umsetzung. Die Redaktion von c’t stellt das redaktionelle Programm zusammen und bietet mit der Konferenz eine unabhängige Plattform für den fachlichen Austausch und Networking.

Zu den Speakern auf der ersten Public IT Ende Oktober gehörten unter anderem Stefan Latuski (CIO der Bundesagentur für Arbeit), Dr. Alexander Georgiadis (CIO des Landes Niedersachsen), Bianca Kastl (Stadt Frankfurt am Main), Thorsten Rode (Stadt Nettetal), Dr. Patrick Grete (BSI), Dr. Lina Harispuru (Stadt Nürnberg), Harald Joos (DRV Bund), Dr. Michael Wissen (Innenministerium Baden-Württemberg), Michael Pfleger (FITKO) und Simone Conrad (Govdigital).

Frühbucher-Tickets jetzt erhältlich

Tickets für die Public IT sind ab sofort über die Webseite der Konferenz erhältlich. Beschäftigte aus Behörden zahlen aktuell 249 Euro (zzgl. 19% MwSt.). Der Blind-Bird-Preis für Teilnehmer aus der Wirtschaft liegt bei 849 Euro (zzgl. 19% MwSt.).
